Not necessarily. Within computer hardware, binary data on the physical level is generally on a spectrum, it's just that a medium and methodology is used that usually prevents data from falling within the middle of the spectrum. So if the value of the bit is within the general range from 0.00-0.33, it's interpreted as 0 and if the general range is between about 0.67 to 1.00, then it's evaluated as 1. The way that the data is written makes values between roughly 0.32 and 0.66 very unlikely to occur, but if there's a hardware problem, a value in that range could potentially be written or misread to be within that range. If that occurs, then the bit is evaluated as being corrupt and the actual value is lost or unknown. If you had different firmware or potentially different hardware that was able to return the raw value, you might be able to guess the value by rounding it, but if the nature of whatever corrupted the bit is such that it may have switched the value from one side to the other but insufficiently to fully set the bit, then you'll be incorrect in your evaluation when you round the value. If you flip a bit in one place, the nature of tight magnetism is such that flipping the bit may likely change the raw value of other nearby bits, but if the medium is designed well, then although the nearby bits may be changed slightly, no amount of switching the neighboring bit will cause the other bits to switch to the opposite or corrupt raw values. The ranges I gave are simply to simplify the example, I don't know offhand how much raw bit values are allowed to vary.
